why: Valid and genuinely large: 64 megapixels in a file of a few kilobytes. Allowed by the guard and too big for the canvas engine, so it must be handed to libvips and convert, without the tab running out of memory.
The outer checksum is right; the one inside the compressed data, which is only checked after everything has been decompressed, is wrong.
Twice as many rows as the header declares. A reader that writes what it is given, instead of what it allocated for, writes past the end of its buffer.
A two-colour palette, and pixels that all ask for colour number 200. A reader that looks it up without checking reads memory that is not the palette.
A palette of seven bytes. Colours take three bytes each, so the last one is cut short.
Two colours in the palette, and 256 transparency entries for them.
Contains a chunk marked as essential that no reader knows. The format says a reader that does not understand an essential chunk must give up.
The header says the rows are interlaced; the data is laid out as if they were not.
A sound picture with a colour profile that expands to 64 MB of nothing. Unlike a comment, a profile is something a reader wants to load.
Valid, with the image data split into one chunk per byte: thousands of chunks, each with its own header and checksum, to make a reader do a great deal of work for very little.
Valid, with five thousand comments ahead of the picture.
Declares a gamma of zero, which a reader that applies it divides by.
Announces itself as an animation of a million frames and contains one picture. A reader that allocates per announced frame runs out of memory.
Valid, with its rows interlaced in seven passes, the way PNGs were saved for slow connections.

why: Names that mean something to JavaScript. A careless reader lets them change how every object in the program behaves; here they are only names.
